section.title: Ephraim and Manasseh
section.sectionRationale: The two tribes of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, receive their inheritance in the central highlands. The daughters of Zelophehad rightly claim their portion by faith in God's command; but both tribes fail to drive out the Canaanites, and then the house of Joseph complains that their allotment is too small, only to be told by Joshua to trust God and clear and conquer the land they already have. It is one movement, the inheritance of Joseph, contrasting believing initiative with faithless complaint.
section.thesis: God gives Joseph an ample inheritance, and the daughters of Zelophehad show faith that lays hold of it, but the tribes' failure to drive out the Canaanites and their grumbling about too little land expose a faithlessness that shrinks back from the very conquest God had promised to bless, so that the fault lies not in God's gift but in their unwillingness to trust and act.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Ephraim's borders and its failure at Gezer, 16:1 to 10; Manasseh's allotment and the faith of Zelophehad's daughters, 17:1 to 6; Manasseh's territory and failure to drive out the Canaanites, 17:7 to 13; and the house of Joseph's complaint answered by Joshua's challenge, 17:14 to 18.

units.label: Ephraim's borders and failure at Gezer
units.note: they did not drive out the Canaanites in Gezer

verses.text: The allotment for the descendants of Joseph extended from the Jordan at Jericho to the waters of Jericho on the east, through the wilderness that goes up from Jericho into the hill country of Bethel.
It went on from Bethel (that is, Luz) and proceeded to the border of the Archites in Ataroth.
Then it descended westward to the border of the Japhletites as far as the border of Lower Beth-horon and on to Gezer, and it ended at the Sea.
So Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, received their {{nachalah|inheritance}}.
This was the territory of the descendants of Ephraim by their clans: The border of their inheritance went from Ataroth-addar in the east to Upper Beth-horon
and out toward the Sea. From Michmethath on the north it turned eastward toward Taanath-shiloh and passed by it to Janoah on the east.
From Janoah it went down to Ataroth and Naarah, and then reached Jericho and came out at the Jordan.
From Tappuah the border went westward to the Brook of Kanah and ended at the Sea. This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Ephraim,
along with all the cities and villages set apart for the descendants of Ephraim within the inheritance of Manasseh.
But they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer. So the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites to this day, but they are forced laborers.

units.label: Manasseh's allotment and the daughters of Zelophehad
units.note: the LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance

verses.text: Now this was the allotment for the tribe of Manasseh as Joseph’s firstborn son, namely for Machir the firstborn of Manasseh and father of the Gileadites, who had received Gilead and Bashan because Machir was a man of war.

So this allotment was for the rest of the descendants of Manasseh, the clans of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These are the other male descendants of the clans of Manasseh son of Joseph.

But Zelophehad son of Hepher (the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh) had no sons but only daughters. These are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.

They approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders, and said, “The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers.” So Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father’s brothers, in keeping with the command of the LORD.
Thus ten shares fell to Manasseh, in addition to the land of Gilead and Bashan beyond the Jordan,
because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance among his sons. And the land of Gilead belonged to the rest of the sons of Manasseh.

units.label: Manasseh's territory and failure to drive out the Canaanites
units.note: the Canaanites were determined to stay in the land

verses.text: Now the border of Manasseh went from Asher to Michmethath near Shechem, then southward to include the inhabitants of En-tappuah.
The region of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but Tappuah itself, on the border of Manasseh, belonged to Ephraim.

From there the border continued southward to the Brook of Kanah. There were cities belonging to Ephraim among the cities of Manasseh, but the border of Manasseh was on the north side of the brook and ended at the Sea.
Ephraim’s territory was to the south, and Manasseh’s was to the north, having the Sea as its border and adjoining Asher on the north and Issachar on the east.
Within Issachar and Asher, Manasseh was assigned Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor (that is, Naphath), Endor, Taanach, and Megiddo, each with their surrounding settlements.
But the descendants of Manasseh were unable to occupy these cities, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in this land.
However, when the Israelites grew {{chazaq|stronger}}, they put the Canaanites to forced labor; but they failed to drive them out completely.

units.label: The house of Joseph's complaint and Joshua's challenge

verses.text: Then the sons of Joseph said to Joshua, “Why have you given us only one portion as an inheritance? We have many people, because the LORD has blessed us abundantly.”

Joshua answered them, “If you have so many people that the hill country of Ephraim is too small for you, go to the forest and clear for yourself an area in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim.”
“The hill country is not enough for us,” they replied, “and all the Canaanites who live in the valley have iron chariots, both in Beth-shean with its towns and in the Valley of Jezreel.”
So Joshua said to the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, “You have many people and great strength. You shall not have just one allotment,

because the hill country will be yours as well. It is a forest; clear it, and its farthest limits will be yours. Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can {{yarash|drive}} them out.”

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, allotted possession. The sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, receive their nachalah in the fertile central highlands. The daughters of Zelophehad rightly claim a nachalah among their brothers because the LORD had commanded it through Moses, showing that God's provision of inheritance reached even to daughters where there were no sons, honoring His own word.

chazaq.gloss: To be strong, become strong. When Israel grew chazaq, they subjected the Canaanites to forced labor but still did not drive them out. The word is poignant: the very strength that could have completed the conquest was used only to exploit the Canaanites rather than to obey God fully, a compromise of half-obedience born of a lack of resolve to trust God.

yarash.gloss: To take possession of, dispossess, drive out. Joshua insists, despite the Canaanites' iron chariots, you can drive them out. The failure of Joseph to yarash the land was not because God's promise was too small or the enemy too strong, but because their faith faltered; Joshua's charge presses them to trust the God who had promised the land and act on it.

basic.context: The two tribes descended from Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, receive their land in the rich central highlands. A bright spot comes in the daughters of Zelophehad: their father had died with no sons, and they had earlier asked Moses for their family's inheritance; now, on the basis of God's command, they receive it. But a shadow falls too. Ephraim fails to drive the Canaanites out of Gezer, and Manasseh cannot take its assigned cities because the Canaanites are determined to stay; when Israel grows strong, they merely enslave them rather than obey God fully. Then the house of Joseph complains to Joshua that their inheritance is too small for such a large, blessed people. Joshua replies bluntly: you have the strength and the promise, so go clear the forest and drive out the Canaanites, iron chariots and all, you can do it. The question underneath is: is the problem God's provision, or the people's faith?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, mixing land records with two revealing episodes. The daughters of Zelophehad model faith that lays hold of God's promise. The repeated failure to drive out the Canaanites, and the complaint of Joseph, expose faithlessness, and the narrative subtly indicts them: the fault is not in God's gift but in their unwillingness to trust and act. We should read the failures as warnings, not models.
basic.originalLanguages: Joseph's tribes receive their nachalah, inheritance, and the daughters of Zelophehad claim their nachalah by God's command. Yet when Israel grew chazaq, strong, they only enslaved the Canaanites; and Joshua insists they can yarash, drive out, the enemy despite the chariots, if they will trust God.
basic.typology: The daughters of Zelophehad, claiming their inheritance by faith in God's word, picture all who lay hold of the promised inheritance through faith. The failure of Joseph to drive out the enemy warns against the unbelief that forfeits what God has given, a warning the New Testament applies to those who shrink back.
basic.christ: The contrast between believing faith and faithless complaint points to the necessity of trusting God's promise, fulfilled in Christ, in whom all God's promises are Yes. Where Israel shrank back from the inheritance in unbelief, Christ secures the inheritance for His people and calls them to enter it by faith, not to draw back to destruction.
basic.god: God is generous, giving Joseph an ample inheritance and blessing them abundantly. He is faithful to His own word, honoring the daughters' claim because He had commanded it. And He is the God who promises victory even over iron chariots, so that the failure to possess the land indicts the people's faith, not His faithfulness.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 27 records the daughters of Zelophehad first securing their inheritance. Judges 1 details Israel's failure to drive out the Canaanites. Hebrews 10 warns against shrinking back in unbelief. And 2 Corinthians 1 says all God's promises find their Yes in Christ.
basic.oneStory: Joseph's tribes receive a generous inheritance, and the daughters of Zelophehad show faith that claims God's promise, but the tribes' failure to drive out the Canaanites and their grumbling reveal a faithless shrinking back. The contrast presses the lesson of the whole book: the inheritance is God's sure gift, entered only by faith, a faith perfected in Christ.

context.literary: The unit falls into four movements that share one refrain. Ephraim's borders close with the notice that they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer (16:10), and Manasseh's territory closes with the parallel line, that they failed to drive them out completely (17:13). These twin refrains bracket the account of Zelophehad's daughters (17:1-6) at their center, so that a narrative of faith sits framed by two notices of failure, an arrangement that quietly asks which posture, the daughters' or the tribes', actually defines the house of Joseph. The boundary lists themselves read like the legal deeds of the ancient world, station by station from the Jordan to the sea, and this precision matters: it shows that the inheritance was never vague or contested but exactly surveyed and recorded before it was ever squandered by unbelief. The unit opens by naming the descendants of Joseph as a single body (16:1) and closes by addressing the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, as one (17:17), a ring that holds the two tribes together as heirs of one father even while their allotments are drawn separately, echoing Jacob's own decision in Genesis 48 to count Joseph's two sons as his own so that Joseph, through them, received a double share. Machir's earlier seizure of Gilead and Bashan as a man of war (17:1) stands as a foil placed at the very head of Manasseh's section, a portrait of vigorous possession that the rest of the unit, with its stalled conquest and its complaint, fails to live up to.
context.historical: Ephraim and Manasseh held the central hill country, the richest agricultural land west of the Jordan, the very slopes Jacob had in mind when he called Joseph a fruitful bough by a spring, Genesis 49:22. Gezer, left in Canaanite hands here, was a fortified mound guarding the road from the coastal plain into the hills; it remained outside Israelite control for generations until an Egyptian king burned it and gave it as a wedding gift to his daughter, Solomon's wife, so that the city finally came to Israel as a gift from her father rather than by Ephraim's own sword, 1 Kings 9:16. The valley cities Manasseh could not hold, Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo, and the towns around the Jezreel plain, sat on flat, fertile lowland routes where chariot warfare, Canaan's most feared weapon, gave a real tactical edge that hill-country Israel had not yet learned to overcome. Zelophehad's case belonged to a much older legal moment: under Moses, at the plains of Moab, his five daughters had already won the ruling that a man's inheritance could pass to daughters where he left no sons, Numbers 27:1-11, and a further ruling required such heiresses to marry within their own tribe so the land would not pass to another tribe at the next generation, Numbers 36:1-12. Their appearance before Eleazar and Joshua a generation later, in a different land, shows that ruling kept exactly, clause by clause, four decades on.
context.canonical: Genesis had already marked Joseph's sons for a double share: Jacob adopted Ephraim and Manasseh as his own, as Reuben and Simeon are mine, Genesis 48:5, a decision Chronicles later explains as Joseph inheriting the birthright Reuben forfeited, 1 Chronicles 5:1-2. The unresolved refrain of this unit, that they did not drive out the Canaanites, is picked up almost verbatim by Judges, which lists Manasseh's and Ephraim's identical failures at these same towns, Judges 1:27-29, and then explains, only after the fact, that the LORD Himself left such nations to test Israel and to teach war to generations that had not known it, Judges 3:1-4. That later explanation reframes this section: the tribes' compromise was real unbelief, yet it unfolded inside a purpose of God that used even their failure to shape the generations that followed. Joshua's blunt reply to the complaint, that a forest can be cleared and a strong enemy driven out, anticipates the confidence Paul later states outright, that every one of God's promises is Yes in Christ, 2 Corinthians 1:20, and it echoes forward into the writer to the Hebrews' warning not to shrink back from what God has already pledged, Hebrews 10:38-39.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Whoever shaped this account placed two episodes back to back so that Israel would read its own history as a test of nerve, not merely a record of geography. Zelophehad's daughters had no army and no husband to lean on, only a word the LORD had spoken through Moses, yet they walked up to the priest and the leaders and simply asked for what had already been promised, and they received it exactly as asked. The house of Joseph had a large population, real military strength, and two victorious campaigns already behind them in this same book, yet they let iron chariots talk them out of finishing what God had commanded. The author wants a later generation of readers, themselves living with unfinished business in their own callings, to see plainly that the size of the obstacle was never the deciding factor in either story. What decided the outcome was whether the party in question actually stood on the word God had given and acted on it, or let visible difficulty stand in for that word. Joshua's closing charge, that they have the strength and therefore no excuse, functions as the narrator's own verdict on the whole unit: the land was never too small, only their nerve was.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: None of the boundary markers or city lists carry any command for later readers; they are simply the settled record of where each clan lived, useful today mainly for tracing how the promise made to Abraham became a lived, mapped reality. The two narrative episodes function differently. Zelophehad's daughters are not merely described but commended, since their approach rests explicitly on what the LORD commanded, making their action a pattern worth following whenever God's people must actively claim what has already been promised rather than wait for it to arrive unasked. The tribes' compromise with the Canaanites and their grumbling are recorded but never endorsed; the narrator lets Joshua's sharp answer stand as the verdict on both, so a reader is meant to feel the force of his rebuke rather than treat partial obedience as an acceptable middle path. Applying this rightly means separating a family's specific legal claim in ancient Israel, which does not transfer directly into modern inheritance law, from the transferable principle beneath it, that God's people are to press believing claims on His revealed word and to finish, rather than half finish, what He has called them to do.

debates.question: Was the house of Joseph's complaint about too little land legitimate?

views.label: No; it masked unbelief with a grievance
views.case: Joshua's reply exposes the real issue: they had many people and great strength and were told to go clear the forest and drive out the Canaanites, yet they balked at the iron chariots; their complaint about size was an excuse for unwillingness to trust God and do the hard work of possessing the land He had given, so the fault was faith, not acreage.

views.label: Partly practical, but still a failure of faith
views.case: The Jezreel valley Canaanites with iron chariots were a genuine military challenge, so the concern was not baseless; yet God had repeatedly promised victory even over chariots, Joshua 11, so to let the chariots become a reason for inaction was to distrust the God who fights for His people, turning a real difficulty into an excuse.

debates.bearing: Either way, Joshua treats the complaint as a summons to faith: the inheritance is ample and the enemy conquerable with God's help, so the tribes are called to trust and act rather than grumble, a lesson against letting difficulties become excuses for unbelief.

debates.question: Is the tribes' failure to finish off the Canaanites in 17:12-13 simple disobedience, or does it also serve God's own stated purpose of leaving some nations as a test?

views.label: Straightforward unbelief, no divine cover
views.case: Joshua's own words to the tribes give no hint of divine restraint; he insists flatly that they have the strength and the mandate to drive out the Canaanites, chariots included, 17:17-18, which places the blame squarely on their nerve rather than on any limit God had set, matching how Ephraim's failure at Gezer earlier in the unit, 16:10, is reported in the same bare, unexcused language.

views.label: Real failure inside a larger, later-revealed purpose
views.case: Judges states plainly that the LORD left certain nations to test whether Israel would keep His ways and to teach war to generations that had not experienced it, Judges 3:1-4, a purpose announced only after the fact; read together with Joshua 17, the tribes are genuinely guilty even while their guilt is folded into a sovereign plan neither they nor Joshua could yet see.

debates.bearing: Joshua's narrative holds both truths without softening either: the fault for the unfinished conquest lies with the tribes, who are given no excuse, while Judges later shows that God had already determined to use even that unfinished business for purposes of His own, human responsibility and divine sovereignty running side by side without one canceling the other.

study.originalLanguages: Four words beyond those already named carry the argument. The boundary lists lean on gevul, border or territory, a word that recurs so often in chapters 16 and 17 that it becomes almost a drumbeat, the border went, the border turned, the border ended; the same word describes the limits God has fixed for the nations in Deuteronomy 32:8 and the boundary He sets for the sea in Job 38:10, so that even a tedious survey list is quietly claiming that this exact patch of hill country was measured out by the same God who measures oceans and peoples. When the house of Joseph finally states its complaint, it uses two phrases Joshua throws straight back at them: they call themselves am rav, a numerous or great people, 17:14, and Joshua answers that they have that same am rav together with koach gadol, great strength, 17:17, before ordering them to go clear the ya'ar, the forest, for themselves. Their own boast becomes the ground of his rebuke; a people that large and that strong has no standing to complain about a shortage of land, only a shortage of resolve. The verb rendered clear in 17:15 and again in 17:18 is bara, spelled with the same three consonants as the verb that opens Genesis 1, in the beginning God created. Hebrew lexicons treat this as a separate, homonymous root meaning to cut down or hew out rather than the verb of creation itself, so no direct wordplay should be pressed, yet the coincidence is worth noticing: the task set before Joseph's tribes is to hew out of a wild forest a place fit to live in, a small, laborious echo of humanity's original calling to fill and subdue an untamed creation. Finally, the enemy's advantage is named in one blunt word, barzel, iron, the metal of the chariots that so unsettled the tribes, 17:16 and 17:18; iron was still a fearsome and fairly new military technology on the plains of Canaan, and Joshua's answer treats it as no match at all for the same LORD who had already broken chariots and horses at the waters of Merom. Gevul marking out a God-measured gift, am rav and koach gadol turned back on the complainers, a forest to be bara-ed into a home, and barzel that cannot outmatch the LORD: the vocabulary of this unit keeps insisting that neither the size of the territory nor the strength of the enemy was ever the real question.

typology.type: Zelophehad's daughters standing before Eleazar, Joshua, and the leaders to claim a promise made a generation earlier, 17:4
typology.fulfillment: They lay hold of an inheritance secured entirely by another's word, spoken to Moses long before they ever set foot in the land, and their claim is granted precisely because it rests on that word rather than on strength or standing. This foreshadows every believer's confidence to approach God for a promised inheritance kept safe by another's decree rather than by their own effort, drawing near boldly because the promise is sure, Hebrews 4:16 and Romans 8:17, fellow heirs who receive not by earning but by standing on what has already been spoken and granted.

typology.type: Machir's early conquest of Gilead and Bashan as a man of war, set at the head of Manasseh's allotment before the unit's record of stalled conquest, 17:1
typology.fulfillment: One branch of Joseph's line had already fought and won its ground while the rest of the tribe would soon let iron chariots talk them out of finishing theirs, so the chapter opens with a portrait of vigorous possession it then fails to sustain. The contrast points toward Christ, the true leader of His people's conquest, who never lets an obstacle stall His claim on what the Father has given Him, securing to the end what His people, left to themselves, would abandon halfway, Hebrews 2:10 and Colossians 2:15.

typology.type: Gezer, left unconquered here, finally coming to Israel generations later as a wedding gift from a foreign king, 16:10, fulfilled in 1 Kings 9:16
typology.fulfillment: What Ephraim's own strength could not take in Joshua's day eventually came into Israel's hand anyway, not through Israelite conquest but through the gift of another king to a greater son of David. The pattern anticipates how the full rest and inheritance God's people could not secure by their own obedience finally comes as an outright gift through a greater King, since Joshua himself could not give the people the true rest that still remained to be given, Hebrews 4:8-9.

typology.type: The uncleared forest Joseph is told to turn into livable, fruitful land by its own labor, 17:15 and 18
typology.fulfillment: The territory itself is a free gift, yet turning it into an inheritance fit to live in demands real, sustained effort on the people's part, a pairing of grace already given and work still required. It pictures the shape of the Christian life, in which believers are God's own making, created for good works He prepared beforehand for them to walk in, so that a gift already secured is nonetheless entered only through the labor of actually walking in it, Ephesians 2:8-10.

study.christ: This unit puts Christ before us less by direct promise than by the shape of two failures He alone reverses. Manasseh could not hold Beth-shean, Taanach, and Megiddo because the Canaanites there were determined to stay, and centuries later it would be exactly that corridor, the plain that runs past Megiddo, that Revelation names as the place where every remaining rebellion against God is finally undone, Armageddon, Revelation 16:16, so that the ground Joseph's tribes could not fully clear becomes, in the end, the very place where Christ's total victory is displayed. Joshua's insistence that the tribes can drive out the Canaanites despite the chariots rests on a divine word already proven true earlier in the book, when Israel routed chariots and horses at the waters of Merom, and the writer to the Hebrews later gives that confidence an explicit theological ground: Joshua himself, for all his victories, could not give the people the rest God had promised, or God would not have spoken later of another day, so there remains a Sabbath rest still waiting for the people of God, Hebrews 4:8-9. Christ is the greater leader of that conquest, not merely subduing enemies to forced labor as Manasseh did but disarming every hostile power outright and making a public spectacle of them, Colossians 2:15. The daughters' claim, resting entirely on a word spoken to Moses and kept exactly across forty years and a change of leadership, becomes in Christ an inheritance kept not across decades but forever, reserved in heaven for those who believe, imperishable and unfading, 1 Peter 1:3-5. And where the tribes let their own numbers and strength become an excuse for half obedience, content with forced labor rather than full possession, Christ never settles for a partial victory over what opposes His Father's purposes; He presses His conquest to completion, so that the last enemy, death itself, is finally destroyed and every rule and authority abolished, 1 Corinthians 15:24-26. What Joseph's tribes left undone through weak nerve, the true son of Joseph's line finishes outright.
study.god: The measuring of this whole unit, station by station from the Jordan to the sea and back again, is itself a claim about God's character that easy summary can miss: this is a God who deals in exact, recorded, checkable boundaries rather than vague blessing, so that four decades after Moses died, a family with no father and no brothers could stand before the priest and point to a specific ruling and receive a specific portion, precisely because the God who made the ruling does not forget it or blur its terms with time. He is also, in this unit, a God who lets human shortcoming stand exposed without editorial softening: the text simply states, twice, in almost identical language, that Ephraim and then Manasseh did not finish the work, and it never blames the enemy's iron or the size of the task for that outcome, which is itself a kind of severe honesty about how His people actually behave when a promise gets hard to keep. Yet even that shortcoming does not close off His purposes; the very cities the tribes could not hold, Beth-shean among them, remain marked out on the map as territory that is theirs by right long before it is theirs in fact, so that unbelief delays possession without canceling the deed. He is, finally, a God whose word answers excuses rather than accepting them: when the house of Joseph pleads its own size and strength as grounds for more land, Joshua turns their own words back on them as grounds for less patience with their reluctance, since a numerous, strong people has been given both the mandate and the means to finish what a smaller nation could never have attempted. Nothing in this section suggests a God stingy with His gifts or careless with His word; every shortfall traces back to the recipients, never to the giver, and the record is left standing exactly that way for every later reader who might be tempted to blame circumstances for a failure of nerve.

crossReferences.note: Jacob adopts Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, as Reuben and Simeon are mine, the decision that gives Joseph a double portion through his two sons rather than one, explaining why this single family receives two full allotments in the land while every other tribe receives just one.

Zelophehad's daughters first bring their case to Moses at the plains of Moab, and the LORD Himself rules that a daughter may inherit where there is no son; their appearance before Joshua and Eleazar a generation later simply carries out that ruling to the letter.

A further ruling requires such heiresses to marry within their own tribe so that no inheritance passes from one tribe to another at the next generation, protecting the very portion Zelophehad's daughters receive in Joshua 17 from being lost again within a generation.

Judges repeats almost word for word that Manasseh and Ephraim did not drive out the inhabitants of these same towns, showing that the compromise recorded in Joshua 16 and 17 hardened into a settled pattern rather than a passing lapse soon corrected.

The LORD names the nations He deliberately left in the land to test whether Israel would keep His commandments and to teach war to a generation that had not experienced it, a later explanation that reframes the unfinished conquest of Joshua 17 without excusing it.

Gezer, still in Canaanite hands at the end of Joshua's life, is finally burned by an Egyptian king and handed to his daughter as a wedding gift when she marries Solomon, so the city Ephraim's own strength never took eventually comes to Israel as another king's gift.

Joshua could not give the people the true rest God had promised, since Scripture later speaks of another day still to come, and a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, the rest this section's unfinished conquest could never itself supply.

Paul holds together a salvation that is entirely God's gift and a life of good works God prepared in advance for believers to walk in, the same pairing of gift already given and labor still required that marks Joseph's inheritance, promised outright yet only entered by the hard work of clearing it.

study.oneStory: By the time Joshua reaches the hill country of Joseph, the book has already recorded one clean conquest, oaths kept between allies, and Caleb's own bold request for a mountain still full of giants. What chapters 16 and 17 add to that unfolding record is the first extended picture of the gap between a promise fully given and a promise only partly taken, a gap that will widen through the rest of Joshua's closing chapters and then swallow the whole book of Judges. Zelophehad's daughters show what faith looks like on the near side of that gap, standing on a word spoken to a dead father's advocate a generation earlier and simply asking for it to be kept; the house of Joseph shows what reluctance looks like on the far side of the same gap, holding a real promise and a real capability and still finding reasons to stop short. Genesis had set up Joseph for exactly this moment, giving him a double portion through two sons his father adopted as his own, so the size and richness of this inheritance is no accident but the outworking of a blessing spoken decades before anyone crossed the Jordan. What this section leaves unresolved, Judges will state outright: that the LORD Himself used Israel's own incomplete obedience to test a generation that had never known war, weaving even the tribes' failure into a longer purpose without ever excusing it. The line runs on from there through a divided kingdom, an exile east and west of the very Jordan this unit surveys, and finally to a King from Joseph's own line who does not merely enlarge a border or clear a forest but tears down every dividing wall and gives His people an inheritance that cannot fail or fade, kept for them not by their own strength against iron chariots but by God's own power until it is fully revealed.

quiz.q: Why did the daughters of Zelophehad receive an inheritance among their brothers?

options.text: Because the LORD had commanded Moses that they should, and they claimed it by faith in His word.
options.note: Joshua 17:3 to 4 grants their inheritance in keeping with the command of the LORD.

options.text: Because they bought the land from the other clans.
options.note: No purchase was involved; their inheritance rested on God's command, not payment.

options.text: Because their father had been the strongest warrior.
options.note: Their father Zelophehad had no sons; their claim rested on God's command, not their father's valor.
Joshua acted in keeping with the LORD's command, not personal favoritism.

quiz.q: What repeatedly happened when the Joseph tribes met the Canaanites in their land?

options.text: They failed to drive them out completely, at most putting them to forced labor.
options.note: Joshua 16:10 and 17:12 to 13 record the incomplete obedience of both tribes.

options.text: They drove out every Canaanite thoroughly.
options.note: The opposite: they failed to drive them out; the Canaanites remained among them.

options.text: They made peace treaties with all of them.
options.note: There were no treaties; the tribes simply failed to complete the conquest.

options.text: They were completely defeated and driven out themselves.
options.note: The tribes held their land but failed to drive out the Canaanites; they were not driven out themselves.

quiz.q: How did Joshua answer the house of Joseph's complaint that their land was too small?

options.text: He told them they had the strength and the promise to clear the forest and drive out the Canaanites, chariots and all.
options.note: Joshua 17:17 to 18 turns their complaint into a call to faith and action.

options.text: He immediately gave them another tribe's land.
options.note: He did not reassign another tribe's land; he challenged them to possess and clear what they had.

options.text: He agreed the land was too small and apologized.
options.note: He did not concede the point; he exposed their unbelief and called them to act.

options.text: He told them to give up and settle for less.
options.note: The opposite: he charged them to take more by clearing the forest and driving out the enemy.

quiz.q: What was the real problem behind the tribes' failure and complaint?

options.text: Their unbelief and unwillingness to trust and act on God's promise, not any lack in God's provision.
options.note: Joshua's rebuke shows the inheritance was ample and the enemy conquerable; the failure was faith.

options.text: God had genuinely given them too little land.
options.note: Joshua shows the land was ample and could be enlarged; the problem was their faith, not God's gift.

options.text: The Canaanites were simply impossible to defeat.
options.note: God had already given victory over chariots at Merom; the enemy was conquerable with God's help.

options.text: Joshua had unfairly favored the other tribes.
options.note: Joshua challenged them to possess what God had given; the issue was their unbelief, not favoritism.

questions: The daughters of Zelophehad boldly claimed what God had promised. Where do you need to take God at His word and lay hold of a promise rather than passively waiting?
When Israel grew strong, they used their strength for compromise rather than full obedience. Are there areas where you settle for managing a sin or problem instead of dealing with it fully?
The tribes let the iron chariots become an excuse for inaction. What obstacle are you letting become a reason not to obey or trust God?

Joseph complained that their inheritance was too small, when really they had not exerted the faith to possess it. Where are you tempted to grumble about your circumstances rather than trust God and act?
Joshua said, you can drive them out. How does hearing God's you can, grounded in His promise, change the way you face a hard, seemingly impossible task this week?

translationNotes.note: Manasseh is called Joseph's firstborn, and the two Joseph tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, together receive a double portion, the birthright forfeited by Reuben, 1 Chronicles 5:1-2.
The cities of the valley, including Beth-shean, Taanach, and Megiddo, were strategic Canaanite strongholds with iron chariots, which the tribes failed to take.
